outputs.L1:
# The War-Song of Dinas Vawr

*(Polished Rendition)*

The mountain sheep possess more savor,
Yet valley sheep bear greater weight;
We thus concluded it more prudent
To bear away the latter's freight.

We mounted forth an expedition;
We met a host, and brought it low;
We stormed a fortress well-defended,
And struck down those who held it so.

Upon Dyfed's most fertile valley,
Where herds of cattle grazed at rest,
We launched a mighty, sudden sally
To furnish forth our feasting-fest.

Fierce warriors rushed to engage us;
We met their charge and overthrew them;
Though hard they strove to overcome us,
We conquered them, and there we slew them.

As we drove homeward our new plunder,
The king marched out to intercept;
His fury knew no bounds or measure,
Yet by his folk we were not swept.

He fled unto his hall's own pillars;
And ere we led our forces home,
Some sacked his stores of wine and treasure,
While others struck his head from bone.

There, in that strife of wild confusion,
We spilled enough of blood to swim;
We left full many a child an orphan,
And widowed wives in mourning dim.

The eagles and the ravens circling
We glutted well with fallen foemen—
The valiant souls and those less daring,
The spearmen bold, and archers, too.

We carried from that field of battle,
Much to that land's enduring shame,
Two thousand head of stolen cattle,
And the very head of him who claimed them:

Ednyfed, king of Dyfed's dominion,
His severed head was borne before;
His wine and beasts adorned our banquet,
His downfall was our triumph's roar.

---

**Note:** This is Thomas Love Peacock's satirical poem "The War-Song of Dinas Vawr" (1829), a piece deliberately written with jaunty, almost comic rhythm to mock the celebratory tone often found in heroic war ballads—the cheerful meter contrasts ironically with its brutal content. I've preserved this structure and all narrative details while elevating the diction. If you'd like, I can also provide a version that stays even closer to the original's exact wording with only minor refinements, or discuss the poem's satirical context further.

outputs.L3:
# The Raid on Dyfed's Valley

We stood at the crossroads of choice, weighing the merits of the flock before us. Though the mountain sheep were known to carry a sweeter flesh, prized by those who savored delicate fare, our company turned instead toward the valley below, where the sheep grazed fat and plentiful upon the lowland pastures. Practicality outweighed preference; a fuller belly mattered more than a finer taste, and so we set our sights on richer plunder rather than rarer delicacy.

With this decision made, our war band pressed forward into the fertile valley of Dyfed, a land renowned for its abundance. We did not creep in as thieves in the shadows, but advanced as warriors bent on conquest. The host that rose to meet us proved no match for our strength; we broke through their ranks and cut down those who stood firm to defend their homeland. Blade met blade, and shield met shield, but our fury carried the day, scattering those who dared to resist.

Word of the incursion reached the king of Dyfed, and he rode forth in a rage, determined to drive us from his territory. Yet for all his royal wrath, his forces crumbled before our onslaught. Unable to hold the field, unable to muster the strength to repel us, the king himself was forced into retreat, fleeing to the very pillars of his own hall—the last refuge of a ruler whose power had failed him in the face of our assault.

The raid did not end with mere skirmish and retreat. We pressed our advantage into the heart of his stronghold, ransacking his house and plundering his cellars of their stores. The king who had once ruled in pride and comfort met a brutal end—we struck off his head, ending his reign in blood. The violence of that day spread far beyond the walls of his hall; children were left fatherless, and wives became widows, the cost of war paid in grief across the land.

When the dust of battle settled, victory belonged to us entirely. We drove away two thousand head of cattle, wealth beyond measure, and carried with us the severed head of Ednyfed, King of Dyfed, as a grim trophy of our conquest. That night, we feasted upon his wine and his beasts, turning the very substance of his former glory into the fuel of our celebration. His downfall became our triumph, his loss the measure of our victory, as we toasted our success with what had once been his to command.
outputs.L4:
# The Raid on Dyfed's Valley

*An expansion in the manner of early Welsh heroic verse*

---

The war-band gathered at dawn's first grey light, spears catching the pale sun like teeth bared in hunger. Word had traveled through the mead-halls of the north that Dyfed's valleys ran thick with cattle grown fat on summer grass—herds heavy-flanked and slow, tended by men who did not yet know that steel was already being sharpened for their slaughter.

They came down from the hill country in a column that moved like a single beast, shields overlapping, the rhythm of their march a promise of violence to come. The valley opened before them green and unsuspecting, smoke rising lazily from the thatched roofs of the settlements below, cattle lowing in their pens, unaware that this would be their final peaceful morning.

The defenders of Dyfed rallied swiftly enough—men snatching up spears and axes, forming what lines they could in the chaos of the alarm bells and shouting. But they were farmers and herdsmen first, warriors second, and against the disciplined fury of the raiding host they could not hold. The battle-lines broke like dry kindling. Blood soaked into the black earth of the valley floor as the invaders cut through resistance with the practiced ease of men who had done this before and would do it again.

By midday the king's hall itself lay open to them, its doors splintered, its hearth-fire scattered across the floor in embers that caught the fallen thatch and began to smoke toward flame. The king had fought—this much the songs would grant him—but fighting was not enough against the tide that had come for his valley's wealth. He fell before his own high seat, and it was there, amid the wreckage of his feasting-hall, that the final blow came: his head struck from his shoulders, held aloft still dripping as proof of the day's work and the valley's conquest.

The plunder that followed was the true measure of the raid's success. Two thousand head of cattle—lowing, terrified, driven now by new masters—were gathered from the pastures and pens of the broken kingdom. The king's severed head was mounted on a spear-point, carried back through the hill country as a grim standard, a trophy to be shown in every hall the war-band passed through on their triumphant return.

There was no mourning in the poem for what had been done, no lament for the fallen king or the burned halls or the widows left in the wreckage of Dyfed's valley. Instead there was feasting—the fatted cattle themselves providing meat for the victory-feast, washed down with mead poured freely as the scops took up their harps to sing of the day's glory. The king's head, they sang, had been worth more as a trophy than his living body had ever been worth as a ruler. The blood that had soaked the valley floor was recast in verse as the price of honor paid, the cattle-lowing turned to the lowing of tribute, and the whole bloody business of conquest transformed—as such things were transformed in the halls of the victors—into a tale fit for the telling, a triumph fit for the singing, cause not for grief but for the raising of horns and the striking of harp-strings long into the night.
outputs.L5:
# The, But, And

The world moves in threes—beginnings, complications, resolutions. We tell stories this way instinctively, reaching for these three small words to carry the weight of our thoughts.

**The** sets the stage. The morning light through the window. The quiet before a decision. The weight of memory sitting on someone's chest. When we begin with "the," we are pointing at something specific, something already understood between speaker and listener. It assumes shared knowledge, a common ground from which everything else can grow.

**But** is the word of resistance, the small hinge on which entire narratives turn. She wanted to leave. But something held her back. The plan was perfect. But plans rarely survive contact with reality. This word carries doubt in its very sound—a soft exhale of hesitation. It is the pivot point where certainty meets its shadow, where what we expect collides with what actually happens. Without "but," stories would be flat, predictable, lifeless. It is the word that makes room for surprise.

**And** is different altogether. Where "but" divides, "and" connects. It is generous, accumulating, endlessly additive. The rain fell, and the streets grew quiet, and somewhere a door closed softly. This word never wants the sentence to end; it keeps reaching forward, gathering more experience, more detail, more life into its embrace. "And" is patient. It doesn't argue or contradict—it simply continues.

Together, these three words form a kind of grammar for existence itself. The moment arrives. But we are never fully ready for it. And still, we move forward anyway, carried by momentum, by hope, by the simple necessity of continuing.

Perhaps this is why children learn to tell stories with these words before anything else—not because they are simple, but because they are essential. The beginning. The complication. The connection that keeps everything moving. Three small words, doing the quiet work of holding our sentences, our stories, our lives together.

**The War-Song of Dinas Vawr**

The mountain sheep are sweeter,
But the valley sheep are fatter;
We therefore deemed it meeter
To carry off the latter.
We made an expedition;
We met a host, and quelled it;
We forced a strong position,
And killed the men who held it.

To furnish our carousing.

Spilt blood enough to swim in:
We orphaned many children,
And widowed many women.
The eagles and the ravens
We glutted with our foemen;
The heroes and the cravens,
The spearmen and the bowmen.

We brought away from battle,
And much their land bemoaned them,
Two thousand head of cattle,
And the head of him who owned them:

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rollicking mock-heroic ballad about a Welsh cattle raid, in the style of "The War-Song of Dinas Vawr."
counterfactuals.output:
**The Ballad of the Kine of Clwyd**
*(in the manner of "The War-Song of Dinas Vawr")*

The Gwynedd kine are boney,
But the Powys kine are fatter;
We therefore, lacking money,
Resolved to solve the matter.
We saddled up at moonrise,
We greased our swords with tallow,
We crossed the hills, unwise
To what the dawn might follow.

We found the byre unguarded
Save one fat, snoring farmer;
We left him quite unhardened
By anything much harmer.
We loosed the bolts that bound them,
We drove the herd before us,
And not a soul who found them
Could raise a proper chorus.

The valley men pursued us
With pitchforks, rage, and cursing;
We turned about and viewed us
A rabble unrehearsing.
We slew a dozen cousins,
We widowed half the valley;
We orphaned children, dozens—
But cows don't wait, or dally.

Now some might call it thieving,
And some might call it plunder;
We call it just retrieving
What Wales had split asunder.
For cattle, like the nation,
Were meant to be one herd, sir,
And we, by that persuasion,
Restored the lawful order.

We feasted half the fortnight
On beef both rare and splendid;
Our bard sang by torchlight
Of deeds that never happened.
He sang of Dai the Steady,
Who never swung a blade,
But drove the herd already
Half-drunk and unafraid.

The kine that once were lowing
In Powys pastures fatly
Are now our own, and growing
Our larders' wealth right smartly.
And should the Powys men complain
Of missing calf or mother,
We'll saddle up again
And kindly take the other.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
**The Ballad of the Dyfed Raid**

We rose before the rooster crowed,
with rusty swords and hearts that glowed,
"To Dyfed!" cried our chief, Blodwyn,
"Let's pinch their cows and cause a din!"

We marched through mud, we marched through mire,
one fellow set his boots on fire.
"No matter!" quoth our fearless lot,
"A flaming foot's a battle shot!"

We crossed the stream (we missed the bridge),
Sir Gareth lost his shield and wig.
"Press on!" he cried, though soaked and bare,
"For glory doesn't need spare hair!"

The watchmen slept, as watchmen do,
(their ale, it seems, was rather brew),
we tiptoed past on stealthy feet,
and only knocked out three in the street.

The castle gates were oak and thick,
so Dai the Smith gave one good kick.
It didn't budge, but Dai's big toe
now sings a very woeful woe.

At last we burst upon the hall,
knocked over vases, spears and all,
the king woke up in his silk nightcap,
and asked us kindly, "What's this flap?"

"We've come," said we, "for beef and blood,
your cows, your crown, stuck in the mud!"
He blinked, he yawned, he scratched his head,
then reached instead for his sword—but fled.

We chased him round the mead-hall thrice,
he tripped upon a bowl of rice,
and ere he rose to run some more,
his head went rolling 'cross the floor.

We stuck it high upon a lance
(it wore, we swear, a startled glance),
then rounded up his lowing herd—
three hundred cows! (or so we've heard).

So raise your cups, ye poets bold,
and sing this tale as it is told:
we came, we tripped, we conquered too,
and stole Dyfed's whole bloomin' moo!
